body.objective: Students will be able to set goals for an independent drawing practice.
body.iCan: I can set goals for an independent drawing practice.
successCriteria: I can set specific goals for my drawing practice
I can explore new mark-making and mixed-media approaches
I can track and assess my growth
body.hook: In Art 30, nobody hands you a worksheet. Professional artists set their own goals, choose their own problems and push their own practice. This year you'll do the same: design a drawing practice that takes your skills somewhere new.

vocabulary.definition: Self-directed work where the artist sets goals and methods.
The different lines, dots, textures and gestures an artist uses.
Using more than one material in an artwork.
Trying new approaches without knowing the result.
A specific skill or idea an artist wants to develop.
Judging your own work against your goals.

study.title: Design Your Practice
study.question: How do I direct my own drawing practice?
study.passage:
Part 1, Look back (10 minutes): Lay out three drawings from previous years. Write: What are my strengths? What do I avoid? What do I want to try?
Part 2, Set goals (10 minutes): Write two SMART artistic goals. Examples:
• "By November, I will complete 20 figure drawings in charcoal to improve proportion and gesture."
• "I will create a series of five mixed-media drawings combining ink, tea staining and collage to explore memory."
Part 3, Mark-making experiment (25 minutes): Fill a sheet with a grid of 12 squares. In each, try a different tool or technique: charcoal smudge, ink wash, hatching, stippling, eraser drawing, scraping with a palette knife, string dipped in ink, sponge, dry brush, oil pastel resist, graphite powder, collage. Label each.
Part 4, Plan (10 minutes): Choose the three most interesting results and plan a first drawing that uses them. Write your plan and timeline in your sketchbook.
Weekly check-in: record what you did, what worked, what didn't and your next step.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

study.product: Submit your two artistic goals, your labelled 12-square mark-making grid, a plan for your first drawing and your first weekly check-in entry.

examples.title: SMART goal
examples.problem: Turn "I want to get better at faces" into a SMART goal.
examples.answer: "By December, I will complete 15 portrait studies focusing on facial proportions."

examples.title: Mark-making
examples.problem: How is stippling different from hatching?
examples.answer: Stippling builds value with dots; hatching uses parallel lines

examples.title: Mixed media
examples.problem: What is an oil pastel resist?
examples.answer: Oil pastel marks resist a watercolour or ink wash painted over them

examples.title: Self-assessment
examples.answer: Compare drawings against your goals and note specific changes

practice.q: How many squares were in the mark-making grid?

practice.a: Hatching, stippling and ink wash (also others).

practice.q: What goes in a weekly check-in?
practice.a: What I did, what worked, what didn't and the next step.

practice.q: How does an oil pastel resist work?
practice.a: Wax repels the wet medium painted over it.
To find strengths, habits and gaps.

practice.q: Why do professional artists set their own goals?
practice.a: To develop a personal direction and keep growing.

practice.q: Why is failure useful in experimentation?
practice.a: It shows what doesn't work and leads to new ideas.

practice.q: How could mark-making support a concept such as memory?
practice.a: Faded washes or erased marks can suggest fading memories.

practice.q: Why should goals push you outside your comfort zone?
practice.a: Growth comes from trying what you haven't mastered.

misconceptions: Waiting for inspiration instead of practising
Sticking only to techniques you're already good at
